rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Self-distillation has emerged as a promising technique for improving model performance in modern machine learning systems. We develop the statistical foundations of self-distillation in spiked covariance models by analyzing a broad class of estimators, namely spectral shrinkage estimators. We establish that for spiked covariance matrices with $\rk$ spikes, $\rk$-step self-distillation achieves optimal performance among spectral shrinkage estimators, outperforming well-known estimators in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, we show that $\rk$ steps are necessary for optimality: any $(\rk-k)$-step distilled estimator is strictly suboptimal for $1 \leq k \leq s$. For the special subclass of isotropic covariances, we show that optimally tuned Ridge regression performs best among spectral shrinkage estimators. We also study a federated approach in which multiple data centers share spectral shrinkage estimators and a common server aggregates them to achieve optimal performance. In this case, we find that the best local rule again takes the form of self-distillation, though it differs from the optimal rule when data are hosted centrally on a single server. Together, our results show why self-distillation improves predictive performance and provide a broader statistical framework that connects it to classical shrinkage-based methods. Bio: Debarghya Mukherjee is an Assistant Professor of Mathematics and Statistics at Boston University. He received his Ph.D. from the University of Michigan and subsequently was a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering at Princeton University. His research interests lie broadly in statistics and machine learning, with a focus on high-dimensional and nonparametric inference, empirical process theory, neural network theory, causal inference, and statistical foundations of modern AI. His recent work studies statistical theory in high dimensions and methodology for transfer learning, conditional distribution estimation, learning with dependent data, and preference learning and alignment for modern generative models. Event Category S. S. Wilks Memorial Seminar in Statistics

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Turing-complete blockchain protocols such as Ethereum approximate the idealized abstraction of a shared “computer in the sky” by augmenting the traditional internet with persistent-state and processing capabilities. This technology can, among other things, enable stronger notions of ownership of digital possessions than we have ever had before. Building the computer in the sky is hard (and scientifically fascinating), and requires the synthesis of multiple disciplines, both within computer science (distributed computing, cryptography, algorithmic game theory) and beyond (mechanism design, macroeconomics, finance, political science). This talk will survey some of Tim Roughgarden’s work in the area and the practical impact it has had. Bio: Tim Roughgarden is a Professor in the School of Mathematics at the Institute for Advanced Study, on leave from the Department of Computer Science at Columbia University. He is also the Founding Head of Research at a16z crypto. Prior to joining Columbia, he spent 15 years on the computer science faculty at Stanford, following a PhD at Cornell and a postdoc at UC Berkeley. He works on the boundary of computer science and economics, and on the design, analysis, applications, and limitations of algorithms. Event Category ORFE Department Colloquia

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Statistical inference in contextual bandits is challenging because the data are collected adaptively and are therefore not i.i.d. As a result, classical Wald-type intervals may fail; valid inference may require inflating them by a factor of √d, where d is the dimension of the problem. When the data-collection method satisfies suitable stability conditions, such as those of Lai and Wei (1982), traditional M-estimators avoid this bad behavior, and standard Wald-type confidence intervals remain valid even under adaptive sampling. In this talk, we discuss how regularization in bandit algorithm design can improve the stability of data collection while preserving strong regret guarantees. The broader message is that carefully designed adaptive algorithms can support both efficient learning, in the form of low regret, and reliable statistical inference. Event Category S. S. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Reinforcement learning in continuous time typically models the state as a diffusion. A fixed policy is then evaluated by minimizing the mean-square temporal-difference error (MSTDE), whose high-frequency limit is the expected quadratic variation of an associated martingale. In many financial applications, however, the value function of interest is tied to a continuous diffusion, while the observed state also contains news-driven jumps. We show that with such jump-contaminated observations, the limiting MSTDE objective picks up an additional term generated directly by the jumps. To address this, we propose the Mean-Square Bipower Variation Error (MSBVE). It replaces squared increments of the parametrized value function with products of adjacent absolute increments. We prove that under finite-activity jumps, the limiting MSBVE objective has no direct jump-variation term, at the same order of computational cost as MSTDE. Simulations show MSBVE staying closer to the continuous-process target than MSTDE, and sensitivity analyses indicate that this gap grows with jump size and frequency and does not vanish under finer sampling. Finally, we apply both methods to mean-variance portfolio selection with 5-minute S&P 500 data. Trained directly on raw data, MSBVE achieves the highest out-of-sample Sharpe ratio. Pre-filtering jumps by thresholding lowers the performance of both methods and makes their ranking depend on the threshold level, whereas MSBVE requires no jump-detection step at all. Joint work with Chenyang Jiang, Donggyu Kim, and Yazhen Wang. Bio: Alejandra Quintos is an Assistant Professor and Nellie McKay Fellow in the Department of Statistics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Her research is in applied probability, stochastic processes, and statistical methodology, with a focus on modeling dependence and risk in financial systems. She develops probabilistic and statistical tools for diffusion and jump-driven models, with applications to credit risk, systemic risk, and microfinance. From 2023 to 2025, she was a Visiting Professor at the Instituto de Matemáticas at UNAM. She completed her Ph.D. in Statistics at Columbia University in 2022 under the direction of Philip Protter, where she was a Fulbright grantee, received the Howard Levene Outstanding Teaching Award, and was a finalist for Columbia’s Presidential Award for Outstanding Teaching by a Graduate Student in 2021 and 2022. Before graduate school, she studied Actuarial Sciences at Universidad de las Américas Puebla on a merit scholarship, graduating summa cum laude and as valedictorian of her class. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Optimization and sampling are fundamental computational tasks. Gradient flow and Langevin dynamics give a familiar connection between the two, while acceleration raises a more subtle question. In this talk, we explore how Hamiltonian dynamics provides an alternative common approach to accelerated optimization and sampling. Concretely, evolving Hamiltonian dynamics with periodic zero-velocity resets yields a descent method for optimization, while Gaussian velocity refreshment yields Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for sampling. In this scheme, short integration times lead to non-accelerated convergence rates analogous to those of gradient descent. Longer integration times, combined with suitable averaging or randomization, give a mechanism for acceleration in optimization, in both continuous and discrete time. By translating the optimization proof to the space of probability distributions, we then prove continuous-time mixing bounds for randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with smooth log-concave targets, with accelerated rates analogous to those in optimization. Bio: Andre Wibisono is an assistant professor in the Department of Computer Science at Yale University, with a secondary appointment in the Department of Statistics & Data Science. His research is in the design and analysis of algorithms for machine learning, in particular for problems in optimization, sampling, and game theory. He received his BS degrees in Mathematics and in Computer Science from MIT, his MEng in Computer Science from MIT, his MA in Statistics from UC Berkeley, and his PhD in Computer Science from UC Berkeley. He has done postdoctoral research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and at the Georgia Institute of Technology. Event Category Optimization Seminar

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract : Gradient-flow optimization is usually viewed as an algorithmic procedure for minimizing empirical loss, with training duration selected by validation or heuristic early stopping rules. We develop a statistical inference framework for gradient-flow training. We show that whenever fitted values evolve through a time-invariant positive semidefinite training operator, the output at each time is equivalent to the best linear unbiased predictor under a corresponding random-effects model. Training time then becomes a variance-component parameter governing variance reallocation from residual noise to structured signal. This turns two training decisions into inferential problems: whether training is needed becomes a variance-component test for signal beyond initialization, and how long to train becomes restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation of the training-time variance component. We show that the REML-guided early stopping rule selects the time at which optimized spectral losses become decorrelated from the training-operator eigenvalues. The asymptotic prediction optimality of the REML-guided early stopping time is established for fixed-design in-sample risk and random-design out-of-sample risk. Deep learning models in fixed-kernel gradient regimes provide canonical instantiations for our results. Numerical experiments and a UK Biobank proteomics application show competitive accuracy of the REML-guided early stopping time with reduced reliance on validation splits and repeated checkpoint evaluation. Bio: Zhonghua Liu is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Biostatistics at Columbia University. He received his doctorate in biostatistics from Harvard University. Before joining Columbia, he was an Assistant Professor at the University of Hong Kong, following two years at Morgan Stanley in New York. His research interests include semiparametric theory, causal inference, and statistical genetics and genomics. His recent work explores the statistical foundations of optimization and deep learning, as well as methods integrating causal inference and AI for drug target discovery and protein design. Event Category S. S. Wilks Memorial Seminar in Statistics

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Many AI systems operate in real-world settings that require making sequential decisions under constraints---such as limited resource capacity---while still providing learning and inferential guarantees. First, consider data-driven recommendations for hospital discharge decisions with the goal of minimizing long-term readmission probability. Hospital beds are a capacity-constrained resource that must be taken into account in decision recommendations. Here, we show that policies based on absolute readmission risk can induce censoring and biased learning of patient risks, while simple discharge-up-to policies based on relative readmission risk reduction avoid these issues and enable consistent learning. In the second setting of AI auditing, expert verification of algorithmic output can also be a capacity-constrained resource. We study the use of betting-based martingale methods to design risk-limiting auditing protocols with valid guarantees. These studies illustrate different ways to design sequential decision rules for AI systems that remain reliable under real-world constraints. Bio: Lydia Liu is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Princeton University. Her research examines the theoretical foundations of machine learning and algorithmic decision-making, with a focus on long-term societal impact. She obtained her Ph.D. in electrical engineering and computer sciences from the University of California, Berkeley, and completed her postdoctoral research at Cornell University at the Artificial Intelligence, Policy, and Practice (AIPP) initiative. She is the recipient of an Amazon Research Award, fellowships from Microsoft and Open Philanthropy, and an ICML Best Paper Award. Event Category ORFE Department Colloquia

title: Continuous-time models and variational structure for the edge of stability
speaker: Sinho Chewi\, Yale University
content: Abstract: In non-convex full batch training\, we often observe that optimization happens at the edge of stability: the iterates are oscillatory\, and the sharpness (largest eigenvalue of the Hessian) hovers at the boundary between instability and stability. We describe a continuous-time model for the dynamics in this regime\, which we call the rod flow\, and explain its relationship with the central flow introduced by Cohen et al. (2024)\, as well as with the edge coupling functional introduced by Litman (2026).
